title: Agatha Christie Vanished for 11 Days. Then She Checked In Under a Fake Name.

narration: The world's best-selling novelist vanished for eleven days.
Thousands hunted for her. Then she turned up at a spa hotel, under a fake name.
shots.visual_description: ac9 downs (dawn grade); ac9_volunteer: torch (walks); ac9_volunteer: torch (walks); ac9_constable: torch (walks); ac9_constable: torch (walks); ac9_constable: torch (walks); keyed camera moves, handheld; overlays: label '11 DAYS MISSING', label 'FOUND: A SPA HOTEL'.

sources.claim_text: Guinness World Records lists Agatha Christie as the best-selling fiction writer of all time, with an estimated 2 billion copies sold.

Press reports and later popular accounts say more than 1,000 police and an estimated 15,000 volunteers searched, and that aeroplanes were used. A Surrey Constabulary letter says some press reports overstated the operation, so the figures are narrated as reported.

On 14 Dec 1926, 11 days after she vanished, she was recognised at the Swan Hydropathic Hotel in Harrogate, Yorkshire (now the Old Swan Hotel); a member of the hotel band is said to have recognised her.
She had registered as Mrs Teresa (Theresa) Neele, from Cape Town; Neele was the surname of her husband's mistress, Nancy Neele.

narration: On December 3rd, 1926, Agatha Christie drove off into the night.
Her husband had fallen for another woman.

sources.claim_text: On the evening of 3 December 1926 Agatha Christie left her home in Sunningdale, Berkshire, by car.
Her marriage was in crisis: her husband Archie had told her he was in love with another woman, Nancy Neele, and wanted a divorce.
Guinness World Records lists Agatha Christie as the best-selling fiction writer of all time, with an estimated 2 billion copies sold.

narration: Next morning, her car was found abandoned beside a chalk pit.
Her fur coat was still inside. Agatha was not.
shots.visual_description: ac9 downs (sepia grade); ac9_inspector: stand -> examine -> point -> stand; ac9_constable: stand -> point -> stand -> worried (walks); keyed camera moves; overlays: label 'NEWLANDS CORNER, SURREY', callout 'CHALK PIT', callout 'HER FUR COAT'.

sources.claim_text: Her car was found abandoned the next morning (4 Dec 1926) at Newlands Corner near Guildford, Surrey, beside an old chalk pit on the North Downs; the police letter lists a fur coat, a dressing case and her driving licence inside, and other accounts mention her luggage. She was not there.

narration: Over a thousand police were reported searching, with thousands of volunteers.
Even aeroplanes, the papers said.

narration: Rumours flew. Had she been murdered? Was her husband to blame?

sources.claim_text: Public speculation at the time ranged from accident to murder, and some suspected her husband. No one was ever charged, and she was found alive.

narration: Sherlock Holmes's creator, Arthur Conan Doyle, took her glove to a medium.

narration: Her family blamed memory loss.
Biographer Andrew Norman suggests a 'fugue state', brought on by trauma.
Others suspect revenge on Archie, or a publicity stunt.
shots.visual_description: task force (cold grade); ac9_inspector: arms_crossed -> point_up -> hand_to_face -> point_up -> arms_crossed -> point_up -> worried; camera push/pull; overlays: label 'THEORIES · NONE PROVEN'.

sources.claim_text: The family's public explanation was that she had lost her memory (amnesia).

Theories, none proven: biographer Andrew Norman suggests a psychogenic 'fugue state' brought on by trauma or depression; others suggest revenge on, or embarrassing, her husband (pointing to the name Neele); rumours of a publicity stunt circulated; historian Lucy Worsley points to trauma and a depressive episode.

narration: She never fully explained those eleven days.
Her autobiography doesn't mention them at all.

narration: This December 3rd marks exactly 100 years. The mystery is still unsolved.
